Results and Findings

Tim Ballesteros

2025-03-01

Introduction

Methodology

To test whether an algorithm randomly constructing congressional districts within the typical confines - contiguous, equal populations - I use Ohio as an example. Using the post-2010 United States Census redistricting, population data from 2010 is used in conjunction with Ohio’s 2020 election results, which use districts based on the 2010 Census.

Findings

Partisanship

As a comparison for what a partisanly “fair” district map of Ohio should look like, two allocations of seats using the 2020 vote are calculated: one using votes for the presidential race and one using the party of votes for the congressional race. Both results are compiled at the state level and seats are assigned using proportional representation, assigned using the Sainte-Laguë method. These results apply Ohioans’ votes proportionally, such that the ratio of votes for each party matches the ratio of congressional seats allotted to that party. Between these two methods, each has distinct strengths and weaknesses. The presidential race is consistent across the entire state (and, excluding third-party ballot access, the entire country), removing possible impacts of candidate-specific differences seen when comparing votes for different congressional candidates. Using congressional election results, however, is measuring the results of the actual elections the model is attempting to assess; individuals may vote differently for a presidential candidate - a heavily nationalized race - versus a congressional candidate - historically more tied to local issues. As politics have become increasingly nationalized over the last several decades, however, the impact of split-ticket voters has lessened.

Despite their theoretical differences, both calculations result in the same allocation of seats based on the 2020 results: 9 seats for Republicans and 7 seats for Democrats. Actual results saw 12 Republicans and 4 Democrats winning seats for the 117th United States Congress.

Based on 60 procedurally generated congressional maps of Ohio’s 16 seats using 2010 Census data, the average number of seats won by Republicans was 11 and won by Democrats was 5. Table XX shows the frequency of number of seats won by party.

The random algorithm on average produced a seat distribution of 11 Republican to 5 Democrat seats, which is closer to the expected proportional representation than the actual results.

[DISTRICT COMPETITIVENESS]

Population

Congressional districts within each state are required to have equal populations, though the degree of their margin of error varies by state. Ultimately, districts will have small deviations above or below the target amount due to compiling geographic units of various populations. Ohio’s Constitution, as updated in 2021, stipulates that “[i]n no event shall any district contain a population of less than ninety-five per cent nor more than one hundred five per cent of the applicable ratio of representation” (Article XI, Section 3(B)(1)).1 This allows districts to have a population range of 10% of the target district population as measured by the decennial census, which based on the 2010 Census would be 72,103 individuals.

For Ohio’s redrawing following the 2010 Census, each district was expected to have approximately 721,032 individuals across its now 16 congressional districts. Using the same 2010 Census data, Ohio’s districts in the 113th Congress ranged from 721,031 individuals (100% of the target population) to 721,032 individuals (100%).

Across the 60 generated maps, the districts created with the largest deviations above and below the target population value were 714,681 (99.12%) and 726,986 (100.83%), respectively. All district populations fell within ±1% of the target population. On average, the median minimum and maximum district population values across the 60 generated maps were 716,665 (99.39%) and 725,115 (100.57%) individuals, respectively.

Race/Ethnicity

States are forbidden from use race or ethnicity to politically disadvantage one or more particular groups. However, several states require the creation of one or more majority-minority districts, that is, a district with a larger proportion of Hispanic and non-White individuals than non-Hispanic White individuals. With the strong (though decreasing) correlation between race/ethnicity and voting patterns, separating redistricting based on demographic and partisan characteristics is challenging.

Overall, Ohio’s population according to the 2010 Census was 81.13% White, 12.04% Black, 3.07% Hispanic, 1.65% Asian, 0.18% American Indian or Alaskan Native (AIAN), 0.03% Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander (NHPI), 0.13% other race, and 1.76% individuals identifying as two or more races. (Note Hispanic includes all individuals identifying as Hispanic regardless of racial identification. All race categories are for non-Hispanic individuals.) The proportion of individuals identifying as non-White in Ohio is 18.87%.

Another prominent measurement of racial/ethnic distribution is calculating the difference in the proportion of non-Hispanic White individuals versus non-White individuals.
